topic: The decoy effect in menus and subscriptions (and where it fails)
title: Can a Menu Option You Never Order Change Your Pick?
voiceover: Can a third option you never choose change your pick? In 1982, Joel Huber, John Payne and Christopher Puto studied asymmetrically dominated options. A decoy is an option that's clearly worse than one item, but not clearly worse than the other. Adding a decoy could increase how often people picked the option that dominated it. In 2014, Shane Frederick and colleagues tested the limits of this attraction effect. They found it showed up mainly when every product feature was shown as a number. It didn't typically appear when people actually tasted a drink, or saw a picture of a hotel room. The authors suggest it may be limited to numbers-on-a-page choices. So when options are listed as numbers, ask if one of them is just there to make another look good. Tomorrow: why do you put off things you care about?

description: Can a third option you never choose change your pick? In 1982 researchers showed a decoy can shift choices, but a 2014 paper found the effect may be limited to choices shown as numbers. New psychology short every day on The Psyche Discourse. Source: Huber, J., Payne, J. W., & Puto, C. (1982). Adding asymmetrically dominated alternatives: Violations of regularity and the similarity hypothesis. Journal of Consumer Research, 9(1), 90-98. Source: Frederick, S., Lee, L., & Baskin, E. (2014). The limits of attraction. Journal of Marketing Research, 51(4), 487-507.
accuracy_note: CONTESTED IN SCOPE. The widely repeated Economist-subscription example is not used because its data could not be verified. Frederick, Lee & Baskin (2014) say the attraction effect may be restricted to stylized, numeric product descriptions; it does not claim it never happens elsewhere.
